paras: The threatened lynching of Rafe Bird took place near Pooler, Georgia, on the night of March 27, 1888, when armed men from Pooler took Bird, a Black farmer suspected in the killing of Joseph Gill, into a swamp and threatened to lynch him unless he talked. Under the threat he accused a Black man named Brown, who was seized and then released; Bird was jailed in Savannah and freed in July when a grand jury declined to indict him. The Savannah Morning News reported the episode within its running coverage of the Gill murder under the headline words "His Narrow Escape from Lynching."

On Friday night, March 23, Joseph Gill was shot dead near Pooler while he, his brother Jasper and a hunter named Heywood lay in wait beside a stolen, butchered beef. At the next day's inquest, which found murder by parties unknown, Bird testified that he had seen two men near the railroad that afternoon, one with a musket.

Detective Wetherhorn of Savannah found Bird's descriptions of the two men inconsistent and, learning that the beef's liver was missing, suggested that Pooler residents find out whether Bird's family had eaten liver. On March 27 Mrs. Ferrill, Marion Gill's daughter, visited the Bird cabin, where Bird's ten-year-old daughter told her the family had eaten liver.

About 5 o'clock that afternoon Marion Gill, Ben Rothwell, Joseph Ferrill and Jack Gill rode to the cabin, took Bird into custody and reported finding part of a liver in a wash boiler. By Bird's account Rothwell told him he had a warrant, and the men tied him, took him to station No. 1 on the Central railroad, bound his thumbs and threatened to hang him by them until he talked.

According to the Morning News, "a larger body of men, armed" later descended on his guards, took him to the swamp and threatened to lynch him if he did not tell the truth. Bird said that about midnight his captors carried him a mile into the swamp and said they would lynch him, and that, believing they would kill him, he named "a colored man named Brown" to save his life. Brown was arrested and brought to the station, then let go after Bird said at daylight that he had been "compelled to lie on somebody." The paper later wrote that Bird's "neck was saved" by Haywood, to whom the "enraged posse" listened.

Bird was jailed in Savannah, where he told a Morning News reporter his story and wept as he described the swamp. A second man named Brown, sought by a Pooler citizens' committee, hid because news of Bird's experience had frightened him, until the detective cleared him.

In July the superior court grand jury returned no bill against Bird and another suspect, Abram Edy, and Bird was released. No report of an arrest or inquiry into the men who threatened Bird appears in the coverage.

The episode was reported only in local columns of the Savannah Morning News, as one development in what it called the "Gill murder mystery." Its March 29 headline announced "A Pooler Posse's Midnight Ride to the Swamp with the Prisoner—His Narrow Escape from Lynching," and the paper printed Bird's own account of the threat at length. The same issue described Bird as "a type of the thriftless and slovenly negro" and gave space to the detective's view that his conduct pointed to guilty knowledge.

The paper called the men "enraged" but did not condemn the threat, instead praising Haywood and noting that the posse "felt sure they had the right man." Its first report of Gill's death had predicted that if "indignant citizens" caught the killers, the county would hardly bear the expense of a trial. In July it recounted that "enraged citizens" had taken Bird to the swamps and "by threats" made him accuse Brown.

Accounts differ over who took Bird into the swamp: the Morning News described a larger armed group seizing him from his guards, while Bird described his original captors taking him there. They also differ over who released Brown: Bird's captors at daylight, Detective Wetherhorn on Wednesday, or the posse after Bird was confronted with Brown.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Rafe Bird
bases: Armed men from Pooler took Bird, a Black suspect in Joseph Gill's killing, into a swamp at night and threatened to lynch him unless he talked; he was not killed (A3, A5, A7).

A group of four or more men acting without legal authority threatened to lynch Bird to extract information about Gill's killing, but he was not killed; Haywood is credited with dissuading the posse (A3, A5, A7). It is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

Bird's own jail statement (A3) and the Morning News's narrative and later retrospective drawn from the Pooler and detective side (A5, A7, A10) agree that armed men took him into the swamp and threatened to lynch him, though all appeared in one paper.

framing.detail: The Morning News headlined 'His Narrow Escape from Lynching' and printed Bird's tearful account, but treated him as the likely accomplice, described him as 'a type of the thriftless and slovenly negro', credited Haywood rather than faulting the posse, and had earlier forecast that captured killers would not be tried.
